Women older than 17 provided written informed consent and women between the ages of 15-17 assented with written consent from a legal guardian as appropriate.
Participants were consented to the study between July 5, 2019, and August 10, 2023.
In the ownership index, which asked whether participants had electricity or a 307 generator, farm animals or poultry, and agricultural land, 20% had none of these.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Improving the quality of antenatal care is essential for reducing persistently high maternal and neonatal mortality in Malawi.
Group antenatal care has demonstrated improvements in quality, satisfaction, health behaviors, and outcomes.
However, the impact of community building, one of the model's core components, has not previously been quantitatively assessed.

This study examined the measurement properties of two community building measures, assessed the impact of group antenatal care on these measures, and explored their potential role as mediators of health outcomes.
This secondary analysis used quantitative data from the parent study testing the effectiveness of group antenatal care at seven clinics in Blantyre District, Malawi.
The Perinatal Peer Support Scale and the Provider Connectedness subscale of the Pregnancy Related Empowerment Scale were used to measure community building and were validated using factor analyses.
Results supported a two-factor structure for perinatal peer support (relational support and peer network) and a unidimensional structure for provider connectedness.

Using generalized linear modeling, we found that participation in group antenatal care was associated with significantly stronger community building across all measures when compared to usual individual antenatal care.
Women in group antenatal care demonstrated higher relational support score, peer network, and provider connectedness scores compared with women in individual antenatal care (p < 0.001).
text.formatted: Women in group antenatal care demonstrated higher relational support score, peer network, and provider connectedness scores compared with women in individual antenatal care (p < 0.001).

text.text: However, we found no evidence that community building had direct or indirect (mediating) effects on maternal psychological distress or infant birthweight.

This study strengthens the evidence base for group antenatal care by validating measures of community building and showing that relational support, peer networks, 49 and provider connectedness are important benefits of participation.

Although community 50 building did not mediate the outcomes examined here, the findings highlight the need to 51 further test of theoretical pathways linking group antenatal care to maternal and child 52 health outcomes.

Malawi experiences some of the poorest maternal and infant outcomes in the world, with a maternal mortality rate of 439 women per 100,000 live births and an infant mortality rate of 46 infants per 1000 live births each year [1].

text.text: CenteringPregnancy is an evidence-based model of group antenatal care that has the potential to reduce some of the challenges in antenatal care that contribute to maternal and infant mortality and morbidity in resource-limited settings.

In 2016, Group antenatal care was recommended for research by the World Health Organization, and evidence from recent clinical trials in multiple African countries has found that group care models improve key outcomes, including facility birth and birth planning, antenatal care attendance, postpartum care engagement, quality of care, preparations for birth and awareness of potential complications, family planning knowledge, breastfeeding, health literacy, and mental health [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] [22].

text.text: In Malawi, a CenteringPregnancy-based group antenatal care was adapted and implemented at seven clinics in Blantyre District.
Pregnant women randomized to the group antenatal care intervention received antenatal care in a group setting facilitated by a trained Malawian midwife and community facilitators.
Women randomized to individual antenatal care (usual care) were offered the eight antenatal care contacts recommended by the WHO on a first-come, first-served basis.
While waiting together in the waiting room, they received a health lecture from a midwife.
Then, they met individually with a midwife for a physical assessment.
The full protocol and results from the effectiveness trial are available elsewhere [23, 24].
text.formatted: The full protocol and results from the effectiveness trial are available elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24]</ref>.

text.text: CenteringPregnancy has three core components: healthcare in a group space, interactive learning, and community building, which are embedded in each of the sessions [25, 26].
text.formatted: CenteringPregnancy has three core components: healthcare in a group space, interactive learning, and community building, which are embedded in each of the sessions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26]</ref>.

text.text: Assessments include individual health checks, where women measure and record their own weight and blood pressure and then meet with the midwife to review results (healthcare in group space), facilitated, educational conversations on topics including warning signs, birth preparation, partner communication, and nutrition (interactive learning), and socializing, interaction, and shared experiences with other pregnant women and providers (community building).

Bringing people together in group antenatal care and building peer and provider connections, could transform healthcare and outcomes for women, supported by evidence that social relationships affect health outcomes [27] [28] [29] [30] [31].
text.formatted: Bringing people together in group antenatal care and building peer and provider connections, could transform healthcare and outcomes for women, supported by evidence that social relationships affect health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[30]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[31]</ref>.

text.text: It is achieved through a stable group and time to socialize, which create trust, respect, safety, and belonging.
These, in turn, allow women to be open and share information and experiences, and they grow into peer support and connection with providers [25].
text.formatted: These, in turn, allow women to be open and share information and experiences, and they grow into peer support and connection with providers <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Relationship-centered care is an important part of group antenatal care, and community building is how the relationships among the women and the women and the providers flourish, becoming a source of peer support and provider connectedness [25].
text.formatted: Relationship-centered care is an important part of group antenatal care, and community building is how the relationships among the women and the women and the providers flourish, becoming a source of peer support and provider connectedness <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Grenier and colleagues' theory of change frames group antenatal care as a transformed model of care that fosters a self-reinforcing cycle of increased, higher-quality care, improving health behaviors and maternal and newborn outcomes [32].
text.formatted: Grenier and colleagues' theory of change frames group antenatal care as a transformed model of care that fosters a self-reinforcing cycle of increased, higher-quality care, improving health behaviors and maternal and newborn outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[32]</ref>.

text.text: Group antenatal care has been shown to improve satisfaction and key outcomes, while also fostering trust and building relationships and community among participants.

However, few studies have directly measured community building within group to determine the effectiveness of a group antenatal care intervention on mothers and infants' outcomes of birth weight and maternal mental health, compared to individual prenatal visits with midwife in Malawi.
The protocol and results of the parent study are published elsewhere [23, 24].

text.text: The data were first accessed on 06/19/2024.
The parent study was implemented at seven antenatal care clinics in Blantyre District in Malawi, which is in the southern region of Malawi.
Blantyre District is the home of the second largest city in Malawi and includes peri-urban and rural areas surrounding the city.
The seven government-funded health centers provide health care to socioeconomically diverse populations from rural, peri-urban, and urban communities.
The clinics also differed in the annual numbers of prenatal patients and midwives.

Government funded clinics provide free health care to the populations they serve but also face substantial health workforce shortages, where only 40% of the national midwife positions are filled and there are only 1.48 health workers per 1,000 people, compared to the WHO's minimum recommendation of 4.45 health workers per 1,000 people [33, 34].

text.text: Recruitment, Enrollment, and Consent: After a woman's initial prenatal appointment, the midwives referred her to the parent study's research assistants to learn about the study.
If the women expressed interest, she was screened for eligibility.
Pregnant women who were less than 24 weeks gestation, 15 years of age or older, and able to consent were eligible for the study.

Conceptually, these measures capture the peer and provider dimensions of community building.
Both measures were left-skewed with limited variance, suggesting a ceiling effect in community building.
The attempt to combine the measures into one overall community-building score through higher order factor analysis was not successful as they did not converge.
This suggests the two measures capture different, though related, parts of community building.
While this study examined the construct validity using exploratory factor analysis, it did not address other aspects of validity.

This study focuses on community building within group antenatal care, using measures that assess the experiences of relational connections and support within group antenatal care.

Social support has also been used in the group antenatal care literature, with mixed findings: with some evidence of increased reliance on peer networks and improved psychological quality of life, but limited evidence that general social support mediates health outcomes [21, 55, 56].

text.text: There is an important difference between what these instruments are measuring, as these community building measure focus specifically on the experience of connecting to peers and providers during antenatal care, whereas social support is a perceived measure of support generally.
This study found a significant relationship between participation in group antenatal care and perinatal peer support (relational support and peer network), as well as provider connectedness.
These findings align with the theoretical premise that group antenatal care fosters social connections and trust among participants as well as between women and providers.
Grenier and colleagues' theory of change identifies community building as one component of a broader transformation in providing group antenatal care.

Together with increased time, decreased hierarchy, interactive learning, self-assessment, and continuity of care, community building is expected to lead to supportive relationships, better communication, empowered partnerships, and more meaningful care.

These transformed experiences may contribute to a self-reinforcing cycle of more and better care, and through improved health behaviours, communication, and service use, create opportunities for improved maternal and newborn outcomes [32].
text.formatted: These transformed experiences may contribute to a self-reinforcing cycle of more and better care, and through improved health behaviours, communication, and service use, create opportunities for improved maternal and newborn outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[32]</ref>.

text.text: The peer support and provider connectedness measures examined here capture dimensions of this theory of change, but not the full mechanisms outlined.
Accordingly, the mediation analysis tests one specific pathway, not the full theory of change.
However, the findings on community building remain mixed.

In pilot RCTs in Malawi and Tanzania, significantly higher community building was found using measures of provider connectedness and peer connectedness, while a quasiexperimental study in Tanzania did not find significant differences between those in group and individual antenatal care on community building [36, 57].

text.text: The literature in group antenatal care has mixed findings on social support outcomes, with one study in the US finding that group antenatal care participants were significantly more likely to depend on friendship or peer networks for social support (OR 2.81), while two studies did not find significant differences in social support between those in group and individual care [21, 55, 56].

text.text: In the present analyses, these specific measures of community building did not mediate the relationship between group antenatal care participation and maternal psychological distress or infant birthweight.

The study demonstrating higher social support among those receiving group care also found that the social support mediated the relationship between group antenatal care and psychological quality of life, while another study found that social support did not mediate the relationship between care and postpartum depression by intervention group [55, 58].

text.text: A future area of research could explore the pathway from community building to social support to health outcomes or through other more intermediate ways like knowledge change, engagement in care, or health behavior not included in the analyses.

This study adds to the growing literature on group antenatal care by establishing the validity of the Perinatal Peer Support Scale, with two distinct domains of relational support and peer network, and the Provider Connectedness scale within the Malawian context.
The findings demonstrate significant improvements in these community building measures among women who participated in group antenatal care compared with those in individual care.

Although the mediation analysis did not yield significant indirect effects on maternal psychological distress or infant birthweight, these results underscore the importance of continuing to develop and test theoretical models that link the core components of community building, such as trust, engagement, and social connectedness, to maternal and infant health outcomes as well as more proximal outcomes.

Building and refining such models will be essential for understanding how community building in group antenatal care leads to changes in outcomes, through the strengthening of social relationships and collective efficacy among women, providers, and communities.
This study contributes to the growing evidence that community building in group antenatal care can be measured and is strengthened through participation in group antenatal care.
Validating the perinatal peer support and provider connectedness scales in the Malawian context provides tools to begin to quantify constructs central to community building.
Further work is needed to refine mediation models and develop a pathway linking community building to health outcomes through direct and indirect pathways.
Future research should test longitudinal models that explore community building's relationship to proximal and distal health outcomes.

For practitioners of group antenatal care, the results highlight the value of intentionally designing group antenatal care sessions for community building, fostering bonding among women and linking relationships with providers.

Training for midwives and co-facilitators should emphasize facilitation skills that strengthen community building, and the use of relational care may be an approach that would further advance group antenatal care.

Relational care is an approach to care that prioritizes the building of meaningful relationships based on respect, trust, and inclusivity, recognizing that human connection is essential for wellbeing.

Unlike traditional person-centered care, which can be seen as a collection of needs, relational care focuses on the quality of interactions between the person receiving care, the caregivers, their families, and the community.
The goal of relational care is to foster a sense of autonomy, security, and self-worth for everyone involved in the care process.

The findings suggest that the consequences stemming from community building in group antenatal care can meaningfully enhance women's sense of support, network, and connectedness with peers and providers.
As group antenatal care expands, policylevel efforts are needed to preserve community building as a core component to ensure high-quality implementation.

Furthermore, investing in the expansion of group antenatal care through insurance coverage and implementation support globally, while maintaining the core components of group antenatal care, may expand access to highquality antenatal care and could improve mental and physical health during the perinatal period.

This analysis was based on secondary data collected as part of a randomized controlled trial, which created limitations as the measures were constrained by the parent study design, available variables and measures, and timing of data collection.
Some constructs relevant to community building, such as the quality of group facilitation, the depth of peer interaction, or longitudinal changes in peer or provider relationships, were not captured.

Additionally, the provider connectedness subscale was not originally developed for the Malawian context, which may have influenced item interpretation despite demonstrated internal consistency and factor validity.
Both community building scales were significantly left-skewed.

Although the generalized linear models accounted for these skewed distributions, there may have been ceiling effects, a measurement limitation where many participants clustered at the highest possible score on community building making it difficult to measure true differences.
In addition, the RMSEA for the provider connectedness model exceeded the conventional cutoff, although the other fit indices were acceptable.
Finally, causality cannot be inferred beyond the scope of the original trial design, and residual confounding may remain despite statistical adjustment.

Understanding community building in group antenatal care may help to explain how and why group models work, especially in contexts like Malawi, where improving quality of antenatal care has been found to address high maternal and infant mortality and morbidity.

Without understanding potential mechanisms contributing to effectiveness, such as community building, the scalability and adaptation of group antenatal care interventions may be limited by not understanding when interventions have high fidelity and what is creating improved results.

This study addresses this gap by validating measures of perinatal peer support and provider connectedness to assess community building within a randomized controlled trial of group antenatal care in Malawi and to examine whether it mediates key maternal and infant outcomes.
The purpose of this study was to conduct a secondary analysis of data of the parent trial in Malawi.
Specifically, the current study aimed to: 1.
Measure community building in group antenatal care and its association with group assignment (intervention vs control) a.
Validate the Perinatal Peer Support Scale and Provider Connectedness subscale as a measure for community building b.
Examine the differences between group antenatal care and individual antenatal care on the measures of community building 2.

Examine the mediating effect of community building on differences between group antenatal care and individual antenatal care on maternal (psychological distress) and infant (birth weight) outcomes Materials and Methods Study Design: This study is a secondary data analysis from a randomized controlled trial, "Group Antenatal Care: Effectiveness and Contextual Factors Linked to Implementation Success in Malawi" (Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03673709) , 0/1, Primiparous (0, reference); Multiparous (1) Relationship Status, Binary, 0/1, Not in relationship (0, reference), In a relationship (1) Income quartile, Ordinal, Q1 (0, reference), Q2 (1), Q3 (2), Q4 (3), Weekly income data was used to create the income quartile measure Ownership Index, 3 yes / no questions, Continuous 0-3, Questions asked if participants owned any of the following: electricity / generator, farm animals, agricultural land * T1=Start of intervention; T2=End of intervention; T3=2 months postpartum 213 214 Sample: One thousand eight hundred eighty-seven (N = 1887) pregnant women 215 (less than 24 weeks at first antenatal visit) between the ages of 15 and 42 years were 216 recruited, consented, and enrolled in the parent study.

Furthermore, none of the 414 direct associations between the community building and the outcomes of psychological 415 distress were significant (relational support, 𝛽 = 1.00, p = 0.817; peer network, 𝛽 = 1.03, 416 p = 0.159; and provider connectedness, 𝛽 = 0.99, p = 0.404).
Similarly, in the GSEM for the outcome of birthweight, mediated by community building, the direct relationship between group assignment and birthweight was not significant (𝛽 = 0.99, p = 0.119).

The indirect relationship between group assignment mediated by community building was not significant (relational support, 𝛽 = 1.00, p = 0.906; peer network, 𝛽 = 0.99, p = 0.141; and provider connectedness, 𝛽 = 1.00, p = 0.542).

The relationship between community building and birthweight was also not significant (relational support, 𝛽 = 1.00, p = 0.976; peer network, 𝛽 = 0.99, p = 0.191; and provider connectedness, 𝛽 = 1.00, p = 0.905).
DiscussionGroup antenatal care is an evidence-based model that has shown positive effects during the perinatal period, yet one of its core components, community building, is underexplored.

This study begins to fill this gap by validating measures of perinatal peer support and provider connectedness and using them to assess community building within a randomized controlled trial of group antenatal care in Malawi.
The CenteringPregnancy-based model was adapted and implemented across seven clinics in Blantyre District, where 1,887 participants were randomized to either group or individual antenatal care.
After validating each measure, we found that women who participated in group antenatal care reported significantly stronger community building across all indicators.

However, in the generalized structural equation model examining these outcomes, community building did not mediate the effect of group antenatal care on maternal psychological distress or infant birthweight.
Together, these findings strengthen our ability to begin to measure aspects of community building and show that group antenatal care may meaningfully enhance community building among participants.
